# Advanced methods

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Limitations of likelihood-based inference {.smaller}

Everything today assumed we could [write down the likelihood and evaluate it quickly]{style="color: tomato;"}. That stops being true when

- the model is [stochastic]{style="color: tomato;"}, so the same parameters give a different epidemic every run
- the [state of the system]{style="color: tomato;"} (how many are infected right now) is itself unknown and has to be estimated along with the parameters
- the model is [expensive]{style="color: tomato;"} enough that even MCMC's thousands of evaluations are too many
- estimates are needed [as the outbreak unfolds]{style="color: tomato;"}, updated every time new data arrive

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Overview of advanced methods

1.  [Bayesian inference with MCMC]{style="color: tomato;"}, which we have just done
2.  [Particle filtering]{style="color: tomato;"}, for stochastic models where the state is hidden
3.  [Approximate Bayesian computation]{style="color: tomato;"}, for when the likelihood cannot be written down at all

And, cutting across all of them, [ensembles]{style="color: tomato;"}: combining several models or several fits rather than betting on one

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Particle filtering {.smaller}

A particle filter, or [sequential Monte Carlo]{style="color: tomato;"}, treats the model as a [state-space model]{style="color: tomato;"}: a hidden state (the true numbers of susceptible, infectious and recovered) observed with error. It runs the stochastic model forward as a set of simulations, the [*particles*]{style="color: tomato;"}. At each observation the particles are [weighted by their likelihood and resampled]{style="color: tomato;"}, so those consistent with the data are kept and multiplied and the rest are discarded. The surviving particles approximate the [filtering distribution]{style="color: tomato;"} of the hidden state given the data so far

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### When particle filtering is appropriate

It is the tool of choice when

- the model is stochastic and the noise in transmission matters
- you need the current state, not just the parameters
- parameters change over time, or data go missing for a while
- the answer has to be updated in real time

The filter also yields an unbiased estimate of the [marginal likelihood]{style="color: tomato;"}. Using that estimate inside a Metropolis–Hastings sampler gives [particle MCMC (pMCMC)]{style="color: tomato;"}, which performs full Bayesian inference for the parameters of a stochastic model

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Approximate Bayesian computation {.smaller}

When the likelihood is intractable but the model can be simulated from, [approximate Bayesian computation (ABC)]{style="color: tomato;"} replaces likelihood evaluation with simulation:

1.  Draw parameters from the prior
2.  Simulate an outbreak with them
3.  Compare the simulated outbreak with the observed one through a distance between [summary statistics]{style="color: tomato;"}
4.  [Accept]{style="color: tomato;"} the parameters if the distance is below a tolerance [$\epsilon$]{style="color: steelblue;"}, reject them otherwise

The accepted parameters are draws from an [approximate posterior]{style="color: tomato;"}. The quality of the approximation depends on the summary statistics and the tolerance, and the acceptance rate is typically low, but the method applies to models for which no likelihood can be written

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Ensemble methods {.smaller}

Ensemble methods combine several models, methods or fits rather than relying on a single one:

- [model ensembles]{style="color: tomato;"}: average the predictions of several models, weighted or unweighted
- [method ensembles]{style="color: tomato;"}: combine estimates from least squares, MLE and MCMC
- [bootstrap ensembles]{style="color: tomato;"}: refit the same model to resampled versions of the data

The spread across the ensemble quantifies [model and method uncertainty]{style="color: tomato;"}, which no single fit can show, and averaged predictions are more robust and less prone to overfitting than any single member
